prompt: Write a first-person detective story featuring a locked-room murder case. The story should be tightly plotted with strong suspense.

outline.name: The Call
outline.description: At her seaside apartment, tied to a half-finished bottle, semi-disgraced detective Addie Reyes gets a call from Lieutenant Frank Okonkwo. Voss Institute cryptographer Daniel Voss is dead in a locked vault; the official line is suicide, but something does not sit right. The narrative establishes Addie’s pathological pattern recognition and the sins of her past—the public accusation of Judge Ellery, the ruin of her badge and marriage—before she agrees to come into the storm.

outline.name: The Headland
outline.description: Driving through the coastal storm, Addie reaches the Voss Institute. Okonkwo is waiting; his skepticism of her is tempered by the guilt he carries for vouching. She is introduced to Gary Lomax, Voss's nervous assistant, who frames Voss as a depressed, isolated genius. The institute itself becomes a character—a brutalist building on a headland, with the research vault at its core.

outline.name: The Vault
outline.description: Addie steps into the sealed vault for the first time. Voss’s body is still in the chair, face faintly smiling; a single platinum key sits on the desk. The room is a prison of physical impossibility: dead-bolted door, welded windows, humming air scrubbers, no hidden exits. She records every detail with obsessive precision even as Okonkwo labels it an ironclad suicide.

outline.name: The Feed
outline.description: Addie watches the final seventeen minutes of the surveillance feed. Voss types, alone, untouched, then collapses. Repetition triggers her gift: dust motes reverse direction for three frames at a hidden seam, and the harbor splash is nine minutes out of phase with the tide clock. She declares the footage is a feeding-loop splice—a murder edited to look like solitude. Okonkwo resists her reading.

outline.name: The Deadbolt
outline.description: With Okonkwo, Addie tests the physical constraints. The bolt can only be thrown by hand from inside, the windows are welded, the scrubbers filter only air. Every fact denies a second killer. The pressure builds as Addie contradicts the evidence, and a buried memory darkens the edges of her mind—a child’s game in a room like this. She suppresses it, but the walls feel closer.

outline.name: Judge and Daughter
outline.description: Alone in a corridor, Addie's past erupts in recollection: her accusation of Judge Margaret Ellery, her inability to prove the conspiracy, the public destruction of her career, and Maya Ellery—the judge's daughter—walking away from their marriage. Okonkwo argues that her need to find a murder here is the same pattern-madness that ruined her. Addie knows he may be right, but she cannot stop.

outline.name: The Hiding Place
outline.description: During a last, unauthorised pass through the vault, Addie’s childhood memory surfaces: hide-and-seek behind a thermodynamics panel, her father’s voice, a key in a grown-up's hand. She confronts the panel and sees a false seam she cannot explain. The room insists she has been here before. She leaves without opening it, shaken and angry.

outline.name: The Coroner's Verdict
outline.description: The coroner rules cardiac failure without external trauma; the case is formally a suicide. Okonkwo tells Addie to stand down. Instead, she secures a single night to reopen the physical evidence, trading on his guilt and her old skill. Gary Lomax's testimony about despair suddenly feels rehearsed, though she cannot yet prove it.

outline.name: The Trace
outline.description: In the dark vault, Addie sweeps the bolt track with an ultraviolet lamp. Phosphor-salt residue blooms along the strike plate, and a needle-scratch gleams on the inside lip of the delivery tray. For the first time she has physical evidence that the room was breached—and that the murder weapon was something no one thought to search for.

outline.name: The Tray
outline.description: Addie studies the delivery tray slot: wide enough for papers, too thin for a hand. She reconstructs a mechanism using a blade of salted ice in the deadbolt, the tray as a delivery system, and a spring-loaded syringe nested in a folder. The impossible murder begins to have geometry, but she still needs the timing to work.

outline.name: A Night's Grace
outline.description: Okonkwo catches Addie in the vault after hours. Their conflict comes to a head: he vouched for her and wants to protect her; she needs to prove she is not the paranoid woman the world built her into. He grants her until dawn. Meanwhile, Lomax is seen making a nervous call that does not fit the official story.

outline.name: The Bribe
outline.description: Following the trace of money, Addie discovers a small fortune transferred to Lomax from an anonymous account. She confronts him; he cracks and admits his observation of Voss’s despair was paid for. He swears he does not know the purchaser, but he places the timing the day before the murder. The web widens.

outline.name: The Key
outline.description: The platinum key on Voss’s desk is not just a key but a decryption token—one that Voss was preparing to use on a hidden archive. Addie realizes the archive would have exposed Judge Ellery’s maritime-money conspiracy. The suicide was a way to keep that key silent, and the real victim was the truth.

outline.name: The Storm
outline.description: At the storm’s peak, a brownout cycles the backup power. The vault’s automated door seals itself with Addie inside. The emergency lamp cuts on; she cannot override the heavy lock. Her solitude is total for only a moment before she hears—or feels—a small displacement of air behind the thermodynamics panel.

outline.name: The Hidden Door
outline.description: The false seam she noticed the night before opens. Maya Ellery steps out of the hidden compartment, unhurried and calm. The childhood hiding place was real all along. Maya has been inside the vault all night, waiting to scrub the last traces and retrieve the syringe. Addie realizes she is trapped with the killer.

outline.name: The Waiting Room
outline.description: Maya explains her presence with terrible intimacy: she knew this room as a child too, and she used it to perfect the illusion of Voss’s solitude. She tells Addie she can walk out, leave the file, and make the old story true again: they can run away together. But Addie reads the calculation behind the offer.

outline.name: The Ice Shim
outline.description: Forced to become both detective and prisoner, Addie reconstructs the murder aloud. She details how Maya shimmed the deadbolt with a blade of phosphor-salted ice during a legitimate visit, holding the bolt a fraction short of the strike plate. Voss threw the bolt believing he was sealed; he was only pretending to be locked.

outline.name: The Syringe
outline.description: Addie completes the sequence—the delivery tray, the folder, the spring-loaded needle, the timed transdermal poison. Voss typed lucidly for seventeen minutes before cardiac arrest, his dying spasm twisting his face into a smile. The ice melted on schedule; the bolt slid home only after Maya was gone. Maya acknowledges it without shame.

outline.name: The Lie
outline.description: Maya unveils her true motive: she killed Voss not merely to bury the decryption key, but to prove Addie’s paranoia was madness—again. If Addie was right about Judge Ellery, then Maya’s whole life is built on a lie. She offers Addie one last door: drop the truth, come away, choose humanity over the gift.

outline.name: The Father's Game
outline.description: As Maya presses, Addie’s suppressed memory finally breaks open. She is a child behind the panel, overhearing her father—the vault’s security engineer—explain the deadbolt’s ice-shim flaw to a colleague. Judge Ellery discredited him; he died believing he failed his daughter. The memory is not shame; it is proof. Addie was always right.

outline.name: The Message
outline.description: While Maya argues, Addie feigns wavering. She slides a scrap-form from Voss’s desk and writes TWO IN VAULT, feeding it through the delivery slot before Maya notices. The same slot that carried a needle now carries hope. Outside, Okonkwo, already searching for Addie, catches the paper and reacts.

outline.name: The Ultraviolet
outline.description: The standoff breaks. Addie shakes phosphor-salt residue from the bolt track into the path of the emergency ultraviolet sterilizer, flooding the compartment with blinding light. Maya staggers; Addie disarms her and cuffs her to the archival rack using the mechanical latch of her childhood game. The physical solution mirrors the emotional one.

outline.name: The Override
outline.description: Okonkwo reaches the override panel and opens the vault door into the roaring storm. He finds Addie standing over a cuffed Maya. Backup secures the scene; Lomax is collected from the institute. Addie and Maya exchange a last look—not forgiveness, but acknowledgement. The case is no longer a suicide.

outline.name: The Decryption
outline.description: With Maya in custody, forensic cryptographers crack the data locked inside the platinum key. The hidden archive breaks open: shipping routes, laundered money, Judge Ellery’s signature unfolding in cold evidence. The judge is arrested; Gary Lomax is charged as an accessory for the planted testimony. Okonkwo gives Addie the vindication she never wanted.

outline.name: The Sea
outline.description: Addie leaves the Voss Institute for the last time. She carries no key, no badge, no official vindication; only the resolution of the true locked room—the story she told herself about who she could be. The storm has passed. She lets herself be seen, and the sea is quiet.

chapters.name: The Call
chapters.content:
The sea was eating the town. That was the only way to put it. Slate-colored water clawed at the pilings below my building, and the wind threw rain at the window in handfuls, as if the Atlantic had taken the night personally.

I was on my third glass of something amber, and the bottle beside it was half gone, which was a number I did not want to think about too hard. The apartment had that unmoored feel of a place lived in by someone who had stopped keeping score: dishes in a cairn by the sink, mail I had not opened in a month, a badge-shaped absence on the hook by the door where the brass used to hang.

Six years ago I had been Detective Addie Reyes of the Harbor Precinct. Now I was just Addie Reyes of Apartment 4B, and the only person in the city who still called to ask my opinion on anything was the man who had vouched for me once, and we both knew that debt was costing him.

The phone rang.

I let it ring twice, the way you do when you know who it is and what it will cost. Then I picked it up.

"Reyes."

"Addie." Frank Okonkwo's voice came through the wire like a man walking up stairs: heavy, measured, a little out of breath. "You sober?"

"Define sober."

A pause, the line hissing with the storm. "I need you to come look at something."

"I'm retired, Frank. Retired means I don't look at things."

"You're not retired. You're suspended. Indefinitely. There's a difference, and you know it."

I closed my eyes. The ceiling of Apartment 4B was water-stained in the shape of a continent I could not identify, and I had mapped it a hundred times. That was the problem with my brain. It mapped things. It found the shape in everything—the water stain, the angle of the mail pile, the way a man held his shoulders in a crowd—and it was right so often that I had stopped trusting it.

Because the one time it mattered most, it had been right, and being right had ruined me.

"There's a man dead," Frank said. "Voss Institute, out on the headland. Cryptographer named Daniel Voss. They found him this morning in the research vault."

"Natural causes?"

"Cardiac. Coroner's leaning that way, anyway. No trauma, no struggle, no sign of anyone else in the room. Dead-bolted from the inside. Welded windows. Air scrubbers. The whole thing is a box, Addie. A very expensive box with one man in it and a single key on the desk."

"Then it's a suicide, and you don't need me for a suicide."

"Nobody thinks it's a suicide," Frank said. "That's the problem. His people think he was murdered, the institute thinks he killed himself, and the brass want it to be a suicide so they can close the file and go home. And me—" He stopped. I heard him take a breath, and I knew that sound. I had heard it a thousand times from the other side of it, when a witness finally decided to tell the truth despite the cost. "Me, I keep looking at the tape. And something does not sit right."

The words landed in the room like a stone in still water.

Something does not sit right.

That was the whole disease, the whole curse, the whole reason my badge lived in a drawer now instead of on the hook. Because when something did not sit right, I could not let it lie. I had to turn it over and over until the shape came clear, and the shape had destroyed me.

Six years ago, a girl's body had washed up in the harbor with a shipping manifest sewn into her jacket lining. Maritime money, I'd said. Laundered through the port in plain sight. And the trail had led, the way trails sometimes led when you followed them far enough, to the chambers of Judge Margaret Ellery.

I'd stood in front of cameras outside the courthouse—that was the mistake, the cameras—and said her name out loud before I had the proof to back it. I'd had the pattern, you see. The whole shining geometry of it: the routes, the ledgers, the numbered accounts, laid out in my head like a constellation no one else could see. And when the subpoenaed records turned out to be the wrong records, and the manifest turned out to have been planted by someone I still couldn't name, the constellation collapsed, and all that was left was a detective who had accused a judge on a hunch.

Not a hunch. A pattern. But there is no word for the difference that survives a courtroom.

The department had stripped my badge quietly, to avoid the circus. The city had made me a cautionary tale. And Maya—Maya, who had loved me for the very thing I was—had looked at me across the kitchen table with a stranger's eyes and said, "You don't know when to stop, Addie. You never did."

She was right. I never did. I was holding a half-finished bottle in a water-stained apartment at midnight during a storm, and I had just been handed a case where the official answer was suicide and the unofficial answer was something that did not sit right, and I already knew, with the sick bright certainty of a woman walking into the same fire twice, that I was going to go.

"The tape," I said. "What's on the tape?"

"Seventeen minutes of a man typing at a desk. Alone. Untouched. Then he collapses, and that's it. The door is dead-bolted on the inside the whole time. There is no one in the room with him, Addie, and he dies anyway."

"And that's what's bothering you."

"That's what's bothering me. Because I watched that tape eight times, and I keep feeling like I'm watching the wrong movie. Like someone cut the frames and glued them back together too well. I can't prove it. I'm not you. I don't have the—" He stopped, hunting for the word.

"The disease," I said.

"The gift," he said, and there was something almost gentle in his voice. "I vouched for you once, Addie. At the inquiry. I told them you were the best pattern reader I'd ever worked with, and that you'd made one mistake, and that a whole career of good work shouldn't burn for one bad call. I still believe that." A pause. "But if I'm wrong about you, this time I go down with you. Do you understand what I'm asking?"

"You're asking me to look at a locked room and tell you whether the man in it killed himself."

"I'm asking you to come out of that apartment and look at the truth with those eyes of yours, and tell me what you see. If you see a suicide, we close it clean, I owe you nothing, you owe me nothing, and that's the end of it."

"And if I don't?"

The line hissed. The storm threw itself at the window like something trying to get in.

"Then we find out which of us is crazy," Frank said.

I set down the glass. It made a small, final sound against the table, and for the first time in weeks I felt something that was almost like standing up straight.

Outside, the headland was a black tooth against the sea, and somewhere on it, in a brutalist building with a vault at its heart, a dead man was still sitting in a chair with a faint smile on his face, waiting for someone to look at the tape and find the seam. The name of the building nudged at the back of my skull, the way some names did—Voss, Voss, Voss—as if I had heard it before in a context I couldn't reach. I let it go. I was good at letting things go, lately; I'd had six years of practice.

I had spent six years learning to leave it alone. I had spent six years telling myself the pattern was a sickness, that the gift was a lie, that the woman who had stood in front of cameras and named a judge had been wrong, wrong, wrong.

But I had never once, in six years, stopped believing in seams.

"I'll need a coat," I said. "It's coming down out there."

"I'll send a car."

"Don't. I know the road. I'll drive myself." I reached for the hook by the door, where the badge used to hang, and took down the keys instead. They were cold and heavy in my hand, and for a moment I stood in the doorway of my own ruined life and looked back at the bottle, the water-stained ceiling, the mail I hadn't opened.

"Frank," I said.

"Yeah?"

"If I'm wrong about this—if it's a suicide, clean and simple, and I make a fool of myself again—you get to say I told you so. The whole world gets to say it." I couldn't finish the sentence. I wasn't sure I knew how it ended.

"I know," Frank said. "Drive safe. The bridge over the inlet floods when the tide's up, and it's up tonight."

"I know the road," I said again, and hung up.

The wind took the door out of my hand and slammed it against the wall. I let it. Somewhere out on the black water, past the pilings and the drowned town, past the channel buoy blinking against the dark, the Voss Institute sat on its headland like a cage someone had built to keep the truth in.

I locked the apartment behind me, walked out into the storm, and got into the car. The engine turned over on the second try, which felt like an omen, and I couldn't decide if it was a good one.

Rain hammered the windshield. The wipers fought it. I pulled out of the lot, past the boarded-up fish markets and the shuttered cafés, down the length of a town that had once known my name and now did a good job of pretending it didn't, and I drove into the dark toward the one place on earth I had promised myself I would never go again.

Not the institute. I'd never set foot in it.

The place I had promised myself I'd never go again was the truth.

The truth had cost me my badge. It had cost me my marriage. It had cost me the life I was supposed to have—the brass on the hook, the woman across the table, the quiet conviction that the world made sense.

And tonight, a dead cryptographer in a locked vault was asking me to buy it back.

I pressed the accelerator. The headlights cut the rain into silver needles, and the sea roared on both sides of the road, and somewhere ahead, seventeen minutes of tape were waiting for a woman with the disease to look at them and see what no one else could see.

I was that woman. I had always been that woman.

The world had called me crazy once, and for six years I had believed it. Tonight I stopped believing.

Let the world call me crazy again. It had been wrong about me once. It would not be wrong about me twice.

set.name: Addie Reyes
set.description: Semi-disgraced former detective, currently indefinitely suspended; lives alone in Apartment 4B of a seaside building in a dying coastal town. Possesses pathological pattern recognition she calls 'the disease' and others call 'the gift.' Six years ago she publicly accused Judge Margaret Ellery of a maritime-money laundering conspiracy, the evidence collapsed, her badge was stripped, and her wife Maya Ellery left her. This chapter she decides to stop believing she was wrong and drives into the coastal storm toward the Voss Institute to examine the death of cryptographer Daniel Voss, carrying her car keys and coat but no badge. Emotional state: shaken, defiant, newly resolute. Knowledge so far: Voss found dead of cardiac arrest in a dead-bolted vault with a single key on the desk; a 17-minute surveillance tape shows him alone; official line is suicide; Okonkwo thinks something does not sit right.

set.name: Frank Okonkwo
set.description: Lieutenant, likely Harbor Precinct. Called Addie at midnight from the Voss Institute. Vouched for Addie at the inquiry six years ago and still believes in her gift; carries that debt and guilt and has told her that if she is wrong again, he goes down with her. Skeptical but trusting. Currently waiting at the Voss Institute in the storm for Addie to arrive. Has watched the 17-minute tape eight times and feels it has been edited ('like watching the wrong movie') but cannot prove it.

set.name: Daniel Voss
set.description: Deceased. Cryptographer at the Voss Institute on the headland. Found dead that morning in the sealed research vault, apparently of cardiac arrest, seated at a desk with a faint smile on his face; a single platinum key on the desk; door dead-bolted from inside, windows welded. Official line: suicide. His body is still in the vault as of the end of this chapter.

set.name: Maya Ellery
set.description: Addie's estranged ex-wife; daughter of Judge Margaret Ellery. Six years ago she left Addie after the failed accusation, telling Addie she doesn't know when to stop. Current location unknown; not yet present in the story. Her reappearance and motives are the case's buried core.

set.name: Judge Margaret Ellery
set.description: Judge publicly accused by Addie six years ago of laundering maritime money through the port. The accusation was never proven and destroyed Addie's career and marriage. Not physically present in this chapter; her conspiracy is a hidden thread of the case.

Six years before the story, Addie publicly accused Judge Margaret Ellery of a maritime-money laundering conspiracy after a girl's body washed up in the harbor with a shipping manifest sewn into her jacket. The subpoenaed records turned out to be wrong and the manifest appeared planted; the accusation collapsed, Addie's badge was stripped, and her wife Maya Ellery left her. Addie has spent six years believing she was wrong.

At the inquiry following Addie's collapse, Lieutenant Frank Okonkwo vouched for her, calling her the best pattern reader he ever worked with and arguing one bad call shouldn't burn a career. He still carries that debt; tonight he told her that if she is wrong again, he goes down with her.

Daniel Voss, cryptographer at the Voss Institute, was found dead that morning in the sealed research vault, apparently of cardiac arrest, with a single platinum key on his desk; door dead-bolted from inside. Official line is suicide; Okonkwo called Addie because something about the 17-minute tape does not sit right.

Addie drives through the flooding coastal storm to the Voss Institute headland and meets Lieutenant Okonkwo, who is waiting for her; she must be introduced to the institute and to Gary Lomax, Voss's assistant.

Addie must enter the sealed vault, inspect Voss's body and the platinum key, and watch the final seventeen minutes of the surveillance tape, which she will come to believe is a feeding-loop splice hiding a murder.

The single platinum key on Voss's desk must prove to be a decryption token meant for a hidden archive that would expose Judge Ellery's maritime-money conspiracy, and its silence is central to why Voss was killed.
The vault must contain a hidden compartment behind a false seam (associated with Addie's childhood game), which will later open and reveal Maya Ellery inside.

chapters.name: The Headland
chapters.content:
The inlet bridge was already going under by the time I reached it.

I'd been driving for forty minutes through a town that had stopped pretending to be alive. The road hugged the coast, a black ribbon with the sea chewing at its edges, and the rain came at the windshield in sheets that the wipers could only smear. The channel buoy was out there somewhere, blinking against the dark, and I counted its seconds the way I counted everything—automatically, the way other people breathed.

The bridge was a low concrete span over the tidal inlet, and the water was over the deck when I hit it. I felt the car lift a little, the wheels losing their grip for a heartbeat, and I kept my hands steady on the wheel and my eyes on the far lamps of the headland, and I did not think about the girl in the harbor or the manifest sewn into her jacket or the name I had said out loud in front of the cameras. I did not think about Maya.

The car made it across. The tide was up, but it wasn't up enough to take me, and I took that as a small mercy and drove on.

The headland rose out of the storm like a fist. The road climbed, the trees fell away, and then there it was—the Voss Institute, squatting on the point above the sea like a thing that had been dropped there and left to calcify. Brutalist, Frank had said on the phone, and he'd undersold it. It was a monolith of raw concrete and dark glass, all sharp angles and heavy shadows, the kind of building that made you feel like the architect had hated the sea and built a wall to keep it out. The rain ran down its face in black sheets. Its windows were dark except for a few lit squares high up, and at its heart, somewhere below the ground line, was the vault.

I parked in the empty lot and sat for a moment with the engine off, listening to the storm throw itself at the roof. The building loomed over the windshield. It had a way of making a person feel small, and I was already small enough.

A figure was waiting under the concrete overhang of the entrance, hunched into a coat, a flashlight in one hand. Frank Okonkwo. He straightened when he saw me, and I got out into the wind and crossed the wet lot toward him.

"You made it," he said. His voice was the same as on the phone—heavy, measured, a man who had been walking up stairs his whole life. "The bridge still up?"

"Just barely." I pulled my coat collar up against the spray. "You look like you've been standing here a while."

"Long enough to wonder if you were going to blow me off."

"You vouched for me once. I figured I owed you the drive."

He looked at me, and I could see him weighing the woman in front of him against the detective he remembered—the one who'd stood in front of cameras, the one he'd staked his word on at the inquiry. The rain had plastered my hair down. I had no badge on my belt. I was six years and a lifetime past the woman he'd vouched for.

"You look like hell," he said, not unkindly.

"I've been to hell. It's got a water-stained ceiling and a half-finished bottle."

He almost smiled, then didn't. He turned and led me under the overhang, through a heavy glass door that sighed shut behind us, sealing off the storm. The lobby was dim and vast, all poured concrete and low light, the kind of space designed to make you speak in a whisper. A reception desk stood empty against one wall. Beyond it, a corridor led into the building's dark heart.

"This way," Frank said. "The vault's on the lower level. But first—there's someone you should meet."

He led me down the corridor to a door marked with a plastic placard: SECURITY REVIEW. Inside, a small, windowless room with a table, two chairs, and a man who jumped up when we came in.

Gary Lomax was in his late twenties, with the pale, soft look of someone who spent his life indoors under fluorescent light. He wore a cardigan over a rumpled shirt, and his hands were clasped in front of him like he was holding himself together. His eyes were red-rimmed, and he looked at me the way a man looks at a doctor who might deliver bad news.

"Ms. Reyes," he said, and the name came out wrong, too eager. "You're the detective."

"Former," I said.

"Former detective," he amended, nodding too fast. "Right. Of course. I'm Gary Lomax. I was—I worked with Daniel. Dr. Voss. I was his assistant."

Frank gestured at the table. I sat. Lomax sat across from me, and his hands went to the edge of the table and gripped it, knuckles white.

"Tell her about him," Frank said.

Lomax swallowed. "Daniel was—he was a genius. The real thing. The kind who could hold a whole cryptographic problem in his head and just—turn it over and over until it came apart. The institute built the vault for him. His work was that sensitive. That valuable."

"And you were his assistant."

"For four years. I—" He looked down at his hands. "I was the only one he'd let in. The only one he trusted to hand him a pen. He didn't trust anyone else. He barely left the vault."

"Barely left it," I repeated. "Then he was isolated."

"Completely." Lomax looked up, and there was something rehearsed in the way the word came out, something I filed away without knowing what to do with it. "He didn't have friends. Not really. He'd had a wife once, but she'd been gone for years. He worked. He slept in a cot he kept in the vault's antechamber. He ate in the cafeteria, alone, always alone. He was—" Lomax's voice cracked, a little too on cue. "He was a very unhappy man, Ms. Reyes. I think he'd been unhappy for a very long time."

I let the silence sit. In it, the word unhappy hung in the air, and I turned it over the way I turned everything over.

"Did he ever talk about killing himself?" I asked.

"No. Never. That's the thing." Lomax shook his head. "He never said a word about it. Not to me. And I was with him every day."

"So the institute thinks it's a suicide because he was depressed and isolated, and you're telling me he never said anything about wanting to die."

"Right." Lomax's nod was too firm. "That's what I'm telling you."

I looked at Frank. He gave me nothing, just a small tilt of his head that meant keep going, and I turned back to Lomax.

"When was the last time you saw him alive?"

"Yesterday. Late. I brought him a folder—the daily delivery. He took it through the tray in the vault door, the way he always did. He didn't even open it when I was there. He just—" Lomax's hands tightened on the table. "He looked at me through the glass and said goodnight. That was it. That was the last thing he ever said to me."

"Through the glass," I said. "So he didn't let you in."

"He never let me in. Nobody but Daniel went into that vault, Ms. Reyes. That was the whole point of it."

I stood up. The chair scraped the concrete, and Lomax flinched.

"I'd like to see the vault now," I said.

Frank led me out of the review room and down a flight of stairs into the lower level, and the air changed as we descended—colder, drier, with a hum in it that you could feel in your teeth. The corridor ended at a heavy steel door with a wheel-lock and a small glass panel set at head height. Beyond it, I knew, was the antechamber, and beyond that, the vault itself.

Frank stopped with his hand on the wheel.

"You heard what Lomax said," he said quietly. "Depressed. Isolated. A man with nothing to live for, alone in a locked room, dead of a heart that gave out. It's the cleanest suicide the department's seen in years. Everyone in that building wants it to be that, because the alternative is that someone got into the most secure room on the coast and killed a man without leaving a trace."

"And you want it to be something else."

"I want to know what's true," Frank said. "I've watched that tape eight times, Addie, and I keep feeling like I'm watching the wrong movie. I can't prove a thing. I'm not you. I don't have the eyes for it."

"The disease," I said.

"The gift," he said.

We stood there in the humming dark, and I could feel the weight of what he was asking. He'd vouched for me once, and it had cost him; he'd told me on the phone that if I was wrong again, he went down with me. And here I was, a woman who had spent six years telling herself her gift was a sickness, standing at the door of a locked room where a man had died, and the shape of it was already forming in my head the way shapes always did—the dead-bolted door, the welded windows, the single key on the desk, the seventeen minutes of a man alone.

Something did not sit right.

It had been a long time since I'd let myself feel that, and it came back like a muscle I'd forgotten I had. It came back like a hunger.

"The vault," I said. "I want to see it."

Frank turned the wheel. The lock clunked open, and the door swung inward onto the antechamber, and beyond it, through a second door with a small delivery tray set into its lower edge, was the room where Daniel Voss had died.

I took a breath. The building hummed around me. Somewhere in the dark at the heart of it, a dead man was still sitting in a chair with a faint smile on his face, waiting for someone to look at the tape and find the seam.

"Frank," I said. "Whatever I find in there—you sure you want to be the man who vouched for me twice?"

"I'm sure I don't," he said. "But I'm the man who did it once, and I'm not the kind to stop halfway."

He pushed the antechamber door open, and I stepped inside.

set.name: Addie Reyes
set.description: Semi-disgraced former detective, indefinitely suspended; lives alone in Apartment 4B of a seaside building in a dying coastal town. Possesses pathological pattern recognition she calls 'the disease.' Six years ago she publicly accused Judge Margaret Ellery of maritime-money laundering; the evidence collapsed, her badge was stripped, and her wife Maya Ellery left her. Has now driven through the storm across the flooding inlet bridge to the Voss Institute headland, where she met Frank Okonkwo and Gary Lomax, and has just stepped into the vault's antechamber. Carries her car keys and coat, no badge. Emotional state: resolute, newly trusting her gift again after six years of self-doubt. Knowledge so far: Voss found dead of cardiac arrest in a dead-bolted vault with a single key on the desk; a 17-minute tape shows him alone; official line is suicide; Lomax frames Voss as depressed and isolated but insists Voss never spoke of suicide; Lomax was the last to see Voss alive through the vault door's delivery tray.

set.name: Frank Okonkwo
set.description: Lieutenant at Harbor Precinct. Called Addie at midnight from the Voss Institute and vouched for her at the inquiry six years ago; carries that debt and has told her that if she is wrong again he goes down with her. Waiting at the institute through the storm, he met Addie at the entrance, introduced her to Gary Lomax, and has now opened the vault's antechamber for her. Has watched the 17-minute tape eight times and feels it has been edited ('like watching the wrong movie') but cannot prove it. Skeptical but trusting; determined to see the case through honestly.

set.name: Daniel Voss
set.description: Deceased. Cryptographer at the Voss Institute on the headland. Found dead that morning in the sealed research vault, apparently of cardiac arrest, seated at a desk with a faint smile; a single platinum key on the desk; door dead-bolted from inside, windows welded. Official line: suicide. His body is still in the vault; Addie has not yet seen it.

set.name: Gary Lomax
set.description: Nervous late-twenties assistant to Daniel Voss at the Voss Institute; pale, soft, works under fluorescent light, wears a cardigan. Was Voss's assistant for four years and the only person Voss trusted; claims Voss was depressed, isolated, friendless, and unhappy for a long time, but insists Voss never spoke of suicide. Says he was the last to see Voss alive, delivering a folder through the delivery tray in the vault door the night before the death; Voss said goodnight through the glass and never let anyone into the vault. His testimony has a rehearsed, over-eager quality Addie notices but cannot yet place.

At the Voss Institute, Addie met Gary Lomax, Voss's assistant, who framed Voss as a depressed, isolated genius who never spoke of suicide. Lomax claimed he was the last to see Voss alive, delivering a folder through the vault door's delivery tray the night before the death. Addie noticed his testimony felt rehearsed.

Gary Lomax told Addie that Voss never let anyone into the vault and the only contact with the outside was through a delivery tray set into the lower edge of the vault door; Lomax delivered a folder through it the night before Voss died.

Addie must step into the sealed vault itself, inspect Voss's body and the single platinum key on the desk, and observe the physical impossibility of the locked room (dead-bolted door, welded windows, air scrubbers).

The delivery tray in the vault door must prove central to the murder mechanism: a blade of salted ice in the deadbolt, the tray as a delivery system, and a spring-loaded syringe nested in a folder. Lomax's account of the last delivery through the tray is a key clue.
Gary Lomax's rehearsed testimony about Voss's despair must later be revealed as paid-for planted observation, making him an accessory.

chapters.name: The Vault
chapters.content:
The antechamber was a white box with a cot folded against one wall, a steel locker, and the hum of the building's climate system in its bones. Daniel Voss had slept here, Lomax had said—a cot in the antechamber, a man who never really left his work. The folded blanket was military-neat. A pair of glasses sat on the locker, lenses clean. It looked less like a place a man lived than a place a man waited.

On the far wall the vault door rose like the mouth of a bank, steel painted a dull institutional gray, and set into its lower edge was the delivery tray—a slit maybe ten inches wide and an inch high, barely thick enough for a folder. I ran a finger along its outer lip. Cold. A grown man's hand would never fit through it. I filed that away, the way I filed everything, in the part of my skull that would not let go.

Frank stood at a keypad beside the door, arms crossed, watching me the way a man watches a horse he is not sure is broken. "You want the facts before you go in, or do you want to see him first?"

"Both," I said. "Facts first."

He recited them like a man reading from a card he'd memorized out of duty. "Voss was found this morning at oh-six-hundred by the shift supervisor doing a welfare check when he didn't answer the morning comm. Door dead-bolted from the inside. He'd been in there since last night—Lomax's delivery was the last confirmed contact, and the feed shows nobody else so much as touch the door until the supervisor arrives. Cause of death per the coroner's preliminary: cardiac arrest, no external trauma, no defensive wounds, no sign of struggle. Desk, chair, body, one platinum key. Nothing else out of place. Nothing in the room that didn't belong to him."

"Nothing in the room that didn't belong to him," I repeated. "How do you know?"

"Because we inventoried every object before we sealed it. The inventory's clean. Nothing added, nothing taken." He met my eyes. "It's ironclad, Addie. That's what everyone keeps telling me."

"And yet you called me at midnight."

"And yet I called you at midnight." He turned to the keypad, punched in a code, and the deadbolts inside the door retracted with a sound like a giant waking up. "Forensics is done. The coroner's waiting on a toxicology readout that's taking suspiciously long, which is the only reason it's not already stamped. You have until they decide to haul it out."

"Then let's not waste it."

The vault door swung open, and the room's air came out to meet me—cold, dry, processed, tasting faintly of ozone and recycled breath. The smell of a place that had been sealed for a long time.

I stepped over the threshold, and the door sighed shut behind me.

The vault was smaller than I'd expected, maybe twenty feet square, its walls poured concrete filmed with a fine white dust I couldn't name. High up, above a shelf line, three windows ran along the wall facing the sea—frames, because the glass was gone, replaced by steel plate welded flush, the welds still showing their beads. I walked to the nearest one and ran my fingers along a weld seam. Cold. Continuous. No break, no gap, no trick. The storm was out there, a faint roar I could feel through the steel like a heartbeat, and no part of it was coming in here.

Above my head the air scrubbers hummed—two units, industrial grade, intake grilles running the length of the ceiling, cycling air that had nowhere else to go. I stood under one and listened. Steady. Even. The sound of machinery with nothing to hide.

The room was arranged like a monk's cell for a man with money. A steel desk against the far wall, bolted to the floor. Behind it, the chair. In the chair, Daniel Voss.

I had seen a lot of dead men, and the dead always look like they're keeping a secret. Voss looked like he was keeping one too—a faint smile on his face, the small, satisfied curve of a man who has just finished something. His hands lay open on the desk in front of him, one on either side of a single platinum key. His eyes were closed. His head was tilted a fraction, as if he'd leaned back to rest and simply never come back.

No struggle. No blood. No overturned chair, no spilled mug, no scattered papers. The body was posed in the geometry of a man who had died exactly where he sat, without a fight, without a moment of knowing.

"He looks peaceful," Frank said from the doorway. He wouldn't come in. He'd been through this door a dozen times today, but he stood on the threshold like the room might keep him if he crossed it. "The coroner said the spasm sometimes—"

"The coroner said the spasm can pull the face into a smile," I said. "That's the party line."

"Is it wrong?"

"I don't know yet. I'm getting the room first."

I started with the door. The deadbolt was a heavy steel bar thrown home, its head seated deep in the strike plate. I crouched and looked at it the way I looked at everything—by letting my eyes crawl over the surface until something out of place announced itself. The bolt was clean. The track was clean. If anyone had forced it, they'd left no mark I could see.

The keypad that controlled the bolt sat flush in the antechamber wall; from inside, there was no way to work it. The only way to throw that bolt was by hand, from in here. The geometry was simple and brutal. A man alone in a sealed room. No second hand could reach the bolt. No wire could reach it from outside—no opening wide enough, no gap under the door, no seam anywhere that would admit a thread.

I went to the delivery tray and knelt in front of it. From inside, it was a slot in the lower third of the door, fitted with a flap that hinged inward, spring-loaded. I pushed it gently. It gave an inch, then seated itself back with a soft click. Ten inches wide, an inch tall. I held my hand against the opening. My fingers would not go through. My hand, certainly not.

Papers, I thought. That's all that ever passed through here. That's all that could pass through here.

I did the whole room like that, on my hands and knees in places, my face inches from the concrete, letting the pattern-reader in me run over every surface. The walls were solid—I knocked along them and heard only dead concrete. The floor was poured and continuous. The ceiling was a single slab. No vent large enough for a body, no crawlspace, no false panel, no trapdoor.

A prison of physical impossibility. The phrase formed in my head and it was exact. The room was not a room so much as a proof, a theorem in steel and concrete with exactly one conclusion.

"Tell me what you see," Frank said.

"I see a box," I said. "A very well-made box. Deadbolt thrown from inside, windows welded, scrubbers that move air and nothing else. No hidden exits. No gaps. Nothing smaller than a folder's been in or out of here since it was built." I straightened and looked at the body in the chair. "And one dead man who was alone in it."

"Then you see a suicide."

"I see a room that says suicide," I said. "I didn't say I believed it."

I went to the desk. The platinum key lay between Voss's open hands, as if he'd set it down gently before he died. It was not a door key. It was too heavy, too deliberate, its head milled with a pattern of fine concentric circles like the ridges of a fingerprint, its shaft cut with teeth that had no business opening any lock I'd ever seen. I did not touch it. I just looked, and the part of my brain that mapped things started drawing circles around it, the way it drew circles around everything it couldn't explain.

A key on a desk. A man who dies with a smile. Seventeen minutes of tape.

"Lomax said he was the only one who ever came in here," I said.

"Lomax said a lot of things," Frank said. "He also said Voss never let anyone in. Four years, and the only face Voss saw through that door was his."

"And yet he delivered a folder the night before," I said slowly. "Voss took it through the tray, said goodnight, and died. The last thing that ever entered this room was a folder through that slot."

"That's right."

"Where is the folder now?"

Frank was quiet. I could hear him thinking on the other side of the threshold, the way you can hear a man thinking when he's a cop and you used to be one. "It's on the desk," he said finally. "Under his hands. The inventory lists it."

I looked down. There was a folder there, plain manila, lying under the edge of Voss's right hand, the way a man leaves a folder when he's finished with it. I hadn't registered it as anything but furniture; now it registered as everything. The last object to come through the tray. The last thing in the room that had arrived from outside.

I crouched so my eyes were level with the folder's spine and looked at it the way I had learned to look at evidence—not as a thing, but as a set of questions. When had it been opened? What had been inside? Why had it come the night before he died, from the only man allowed near the room?

"It's the daily delivery," Frank said, reading my silence. "Lomax said he brought papers every evening. Standard procedure for a man who worked from inside a vault."

"Standard," I repeated. The word sat wrong in my mouth. I let it sit.

I made myself step back and turned a slow circle in the middle of the impossible room. The scrubbers hummed. The storm roared beyond the welded steel. The cot wasn't in here—it was in the antechamber, where I'd seen it. The walls were bare but for the shelves of binders and the three blind windows. The floor was clean. The air was clean. The whole room was clean, in the way a room is clean when someone has had hours to make it clean, and then the cleaning crew was sealed out and the room was sealed in with nothing but a dead man and a key.

And that, finally, was the thing that sat wrong.

A man who lives in filth leaves filth. A man who works obsessively leaves the scatter of his work. Daniel Voss had lived in this vault for years, had slept on a cot in the antechamber, had typed and thought and hoarded papers here, and there was not a coffee ring, not a crumpled page, not a single thing out of place. Too clean. Not staged—I couldn't say staged—but too clean, the way a room is clean after the last person to touch it wiped their fingerprints off everything on their way out.

"Frank," I said.

"Yeah."

"Who cleaned this room after he died?"

He blinked at me from the doorway. "Cleaned it? Forensics went through it. Inventory. Evidence bags. That's standard."

"Before forensics," I said. "He dies at some point in the night. Between the death and the find, is there any point where the door is open, even for a minute? Any point where someone could step in here and make sure everything was exactly where it belonged?"

Frank's face did something complicated. "The door was dead-bolted from the inside, Addie. Nobody stepped in here. The feed shows nobody even touched the door until the supervisor came, and he had to call the emergency override from the security office. That's on the record. It's on the tape."

"The tape," I said. "Seventeen minutes of a man alone."

"Seventeen minutes of a man alone," he agreed. "And you can watch it yourself, after you're done in here. It's in the security office, and it's the most boring seventeen minutes I've ever sat through, and it's the thing that's been keeping me up at night, and I still can't tell you why."

I looked at the dead man in the chair, at his faint satisfied smile, at the platinum key lying between his open hands like an offering. The room hummed. The storm roared beyond the steel. And somewhere in the back of my skull, in the part of me I had spent six years trying to kill, a shape was beginning to form—not a solution, not yet, just the first dark outline of one, the way a face forms in fog.

"It's not the most boring seventeen minutes you've ever sat through," I said. "It's the most interesting one, and you just don't know why yet."

Frank made a sound that might have been a laugh or might have been a sigh. "You always did have a way of making a man feel like he'd missed the point."

"That's the job," I said. "Show me the tape."

I took one last look at the room before I left it—the dead-bolted door, the welded windows, the humming scrubbers, the smiling dead man and the key that opened nothing I could see. A prison of physical impossibility, and yet I could not shake the feeling that the prison was the point. That the room had been built, and sealed, and arranged, to prove exactly one thing.

That no one could have done this.

Which meant, if I was right about the shape forming in the fog, that the room itself was the alibi.

I stepped out of the vault, and the door sighed shut behind me, sealing the dead man back into his impossible room, and I followed Frank down the corridor toward the security office and the seventeen minutes of tape that were waiting to tell me the truth.

set.name: Addie Reyes
set.description: Former detective, indefinitely suspended, at the Voss Institute lower level, having just left the sealed vault and now walking with Frank toward the security office to watch the 17-minute tape. She has catalogued the vault's impossibility: deadbolt thrown only by hand from inside, welded-over windows, two humming air scrubbers, delivery tray slit 10 inches by 1 inch with a spring-loaded flap that admits only papers, no gaps or hidden exits. She inspected Voss's body in the chair (faint smile, head tilted, hands open on either side of the platinum key; a plain manila folder — Lomax's last delivery — lying under his right hand). She noticed the room is conspicuously too clean, as if wiped after the death, and has begun to suspect the room itself is the alibi. Carries car keys and coat, no badge. Emotional state: resolute, her gift re-awakened after six years of self-doubt, hungry for the tape.

set.name: Frank Okonkwo
set.description: Lieutenant at Harbor Precinct, at the Voss Institute, leading Addie down the corridor to the security office to view the tape. He recited the case facts: Voss found at 0600 by shift supervisor doing a welfare check; door dead-bolted from inside; coroner's preliminary is cardiac arrest, no trauma, no struggle; toxicology readout is taking suspiciously long; inventory of the room is clean with nothing added or taken. He stood on the vault threshold and would not enter. Has watched the tape eight times, feels it is 'the wrong movie,' cannot say why. Mentioned that the vault door's emergency override lives in the security office. Still carries the debt of vouching for Addie; told her if she is wrong again he goes down with her.

set.name: Daniel Voss
set.description: Deceased. Cryptographer at the Voss Institute. Body still in the sealed vault, seated at the bolted-down steel desk, faint satisfied smile, head tilted as if resting, eyes closed, hands open on either side of a single platinum key. A plain manila folder (Lomax's daily delivery, the last object to enter the room) lies under his right hand. Coroner's preliminary: cardiac arrest, no external trauma, no defensive wounds, no struggle. Toxicological readout pending; body has not yet been removed. Official line remains suicide.

set.name: Maya Ellery
set.description: Addie's estranged ex-wife; daughter of Judge Margaret Ellery. Six years ago she left Addie after the failed accusation, telling her she doesn't know when to stop. Current location unknown; not yet present in the story. Her reappearance and motives are the case's buried core. No change this chapter.

set.name: Judge Margaret Ellery
set.description: Judge publicly accused by Addie six years ago of laundering maritime money through the port; the accusation was never proven and destroyed Addie's career and marriage. Not physically present; her conspiracy is a hidden thread of the case. No change this chapter.

set.name: Gary Lomax
set.description: Nervous late-twenties assistant to Daniel Voss; pale, soft, cardigan, works under fluorescent light. Remained in the institute (last seen in the Security Review room) while Addie examined the vault. Was Voss's assistant for four years, the only person Voss trusted or let near the vault; claims Voss was depressed, isolated, friendless, but never spoke of suicide. Delivered the folder through the delivery tray the night before the death — the last object to enter the vault, now lying under Voss's hand. His testimony has a rehearsed, over-eager quality Addie has noted but cannot yet place.

Addie catalogued the sealed vault: roughly twenty feet square, poured concrete walls filmed with fine white dust, three windows high up welded over with steel plate, two industrial air scrubbers cycling air, steel desk bolted to the floor. The deadbolt is thrown only by hand from inside with no external keypad access; the delivery tray is a slot ten inches by one inch with a spring-loaded flap admitting only papers. No gaps, vents large enough for a body, crawlspaces, false panels, or trapdoors. She also noted the room is conspicuously too clean — no coffee rings, no scattered work, nothing out of place — as if wiped after the death.

Addie inspected Voss's body in the vault: faint satisfied smile, head tilted, eyes closed, hands open on either side of a single platinum key on the desk. The key is not a door key — too heavy, head milled with concentric-circle ridges, unusual teeth. A plain manila folder, Lomax's last delivery through the tray, lies under Voss's right hand. Coroner's preliminary: cardiac arrest, no external trauma, no defensive wounds, no struggle; toxicology readout pending, body not yet removed.

Frank told Addie that the vault door's emergency override is operated from the security office; when the shift supervisor found Voss's body, he had to call the override from the security office to open the dead-bolted door. The feed shows nobody touched the door until that point.
Addie's observation that the vault was unnaturally clean, as if wiped after the death, must later be explained by Maya's post-murder effort to scrub traces of her presence and retrieve the syringe.
The vault door's emergency override is operated from the security office; it must later be used by Okonkwo to open the sealed door after Addie is trapped inside with Maya.
The manila folder under Voss's right hand — Lomax's last delivery through the tray — must be examined; its contents and construction are tied to the syringe mechanism and the murder geometry.

chapters.name: The Feed
chapters.content:
The security office was a glass fishbowl bolted to the end of the corridor, walled in by a bank of dead monitors and a wall clock that had stopped at 4:47 and would never be right again. A single workstation faced the far wall, and on its screen the vault sat frozen, grain-flecked, the dead man still in his chair, because they'd left the feed on the last frame.

Frank pulled a chair out for me with his foot. "Seventeen minutes. I've watched it eight times. I'll watch a ninth with you, and then you'll tell me I'm wrong about something, I'll say you're wrong, and we'll both be tired."

"Deal," I said, and sat.

The tech had queued it up. The timestamp ran across the bottom in green: 23:41:02. The night before. Voss at his desk, back to the door, the crown of his head a gray smudge against the white wall. The camera hung high in the corner, wide enough to take in all twenty feet of impossible room.

"Is there sound?"

"No mic. The scrubbers would eat it anyway."

"Then it's a silent film."

"Seventeen minutes of one."

Frank hit play.

For a long stretch, nothing happened in the way nothing happens: the kind of nothing that glazes the eye. Voss typed, his hands moving in that fast, economical way of a man who had spent decades making thought into keystrokes. Dust drifted in slow tides under the scrubbers' draw. The clock in the corner of the screen crawled. 23:41. 23:47. 23:52. The storm beyond the welded windows was inaudible, visible only as the occasional flex of light along the steel plates.

"Nine minutes in, he stops," Frank said. "Gets up, gets water, sits back down."

Voss did exactly that. He crossed the frame to the small sink, filled a cup, drank, returned. The cup went back. He resumed typing.

And here was the thing I noticed, sitting in the dark with my eyes on the green timestamps: Voss never looked up. Not once. He was alone in the truest sense, the way a man is alone inside his own skull.

"This is where I start to feel it," Frank said quietly.

"Feel what?"

"The wrongness. Every time, right around here, I get the feeling I'm watching something that's too—" He hunted for the word.

"Composed," I said.

"Yeah. Composed."

At 23:53:41, Voss's hands slowed. He typed two or three characters, paused, typed again. His left hand came up and pressed against his chest, flat, as if checking that something was still there. Then it came down and lay on the desk beside the keyboard, fingers spread.

"Here it comes," Frank said.

Voss's head tilted. His shoulders curved forward, and he stayed folded like that for a long moment. Then, slowly, like a tree coming down, he slid out of the chair and hit the floor.

The chair rolled back and struck the wall. Voss lay on the concrete, one arm out, face to the ceiling. The smile—I could see it even at this distance and grain—was already forming, the involuntary rictus of the heart's last cramp pulling his mouth up into the shape of satisfaction.

Then nothing. The frame held him there until the timestamp reached 23:58:41 and the picture cut to black.

"Seventeen minutes," Frank said. "A man types. A man dies. No one enters, no one leaves, no one touches him. The bolt stays thrown." He killed the playback. "So tell me what I'm missing. Because I've watched it eight times and it's the same every time."

"It's not the same every time," I said. "Play it again."

He sighed and hit play.

We watched it a second time, and a third. Voss typed. Voss drank. Voss pressed his hand to his chest and died. I didn't watch his hands. I watched the room: the dust in its slow tides, the light along the welded windows, the shadow under the desk that never moved. Nothing moved that shouldn't have. That was the verdict of the second pass, and the third.

"Fourth time," I said.

"Addie, my eyes are bleeding."

"Mine too. That's the point. When something won't give up its shape, you stare at it until it does."

On the fourth pass I did something I hadn't done in six years, something I'd trained myself out of because it cost me everything: I let the pattern-reader take over. I stopped watching the movie and started watching the frames as frames, the dust motes as points of light, the scrubbers' cycles as rhythms I could count against the timestamp. I let my eyes unfocus, and the film became a machine of light, a long steady hum of sameness—

—and in the hum, at last, a single false note.

"Stop," I said.

Frank's hand froze. "What?"

"Go back. Thirteen minutes in. The wall."

He scrubbed back. "Here?"

"Frame by frame."

He went frame by frame, and I watched the dust. Under the scrubbers' draw, the motes drifted toward the ceiling intake, then fell in a slow spiral back down the far wall. It was a rhythm; I had counted it through four passes.

And at the seam where the far wall met the window frame, three frames in a row, the rhythm broke.

The motes didn't drift. They reversed. Three frames of backward motion, a tiny eddy in the wrong direction, as if something had displaced the air from the other side of the wall—a body moving, a door opening, a draft from a space that did not exist.

"Play those three frames again."

He played them. I made him play them eleven more times before I was sure.

"What am I looking at?" Frank asked.

"Dust," I said. "Reversing direction for three frames at the seam where the wall meets the window. Three frames out of forty-eight thousand. You could watch this tape until your eyes fell out and never see it, because the human eye doesn't watch dust. But the pattern-reader does."

"Or," Frank said slowly, "it's a glitch. Compression artifact. The scrubbers kicking over."

"It's not the scrubbers. I counted their cycle. They kick over every eleven seconds, and the dust reverses on a schedule of its own." I leaned forward. "That seam is where something is. Not a door—there's no door there, I knocked the whole wall. But something. A seam a camera can see and a hand can't find."

Frank was quiet. I could feel him not wanting to believe it, the way you feel a man stiffen beside you in the dark.

"One anomaly," he said. "One. In seventeen minutes."

"There's a second."

He turned to look at me. "Where?"

"The splash."

"The what?"

I reached past him and took the keyboard. My face floated in the dark glass of the dead monitors. I scrubbed the feed forward, past the blackout at 23:58:41, into the next file—the camera had kept recording, catching the antechamber door and, beyond it, the narrow window that faced the harbor.

"After he dies, the feed keeps going," I said. "Same camera, same room, until morning. Watch the window."

Frank leaned in. Beyond the vault's welded windows, the storm threw itself against the headland. Sheets of rain, a gray boiling sea, and in the lower corner of the frame a white curl of spray where a wave hit the seawall below the institute.

"There," I said, and froze the frame. "That splash. What time is it?"

"01:14:52."

"Now watch this." I scrubbed back to 23:58:41 and ran forward slowly. The wave pattern cycled in its long gray rhythm, and I watched the tide clock the institute kept mounted over the window.

The white curl of spray came again at 01:23:52.

"Nine minutes," I said. "The splash that should hit the seawall at one-fourteen hits at one-twenty-three. Nine minutes late."

"Waves don't keep a schedule," Frank said. "That's the whole point of waves."

"They're not random either. Not on a headland with a seawall and a tide clock. I grew up on this water. A wave doesn't arrive nine minutes late and then go back to being early. That's not how physics works."

"Then how does it work?"

"It works if the film was cut," I said. "It works if the splice removed nine minutes and the editor pasted the edges together and didn't bother to make the sea match. A human watching sees waves. A human watching sees a man typing and dying. But the sea knows. The sea keeps its own clock, and the sea is telling me nine minutes are missing."

Frank stood up. He walked to the glass wall and stood with his back to me, palm flat against it like a man testing whether it would hold him.

"Nine minutes," he said. "A grain of dust that moves backwards for three frames. That's what you want to hang a murder on."

"I don't want to hang anything. I'm telling you what the tape says."

"The tape says a man killed himself." He turned. "I've watched it eight times. I've sat in this chair and watched a man type and drink water and die, and I've told myself the whole time it was wrong, because I brought you here and I need you to be right. But wanting something to be wrong isn't the same as it being wrong. You know that better than anyone."

The words landed. They were meant to. I felt them go in, the old familiar knife.

"I know," I said.

"Then look me in the eye and tell me that dust and a wave add up to a murder."

I looked him in the eye. "They add up to a splice. They add up to a film edited to show a man alone. And if the film has been edited, then the edit is the evidence. Nobody edits seventeen minutes of nothing unless the nothing is hiding something."

He shook his head. "This is the old pattern, Addie. The girl in the harbor, the manifest sewn into her jacket—you saw a pattern there too, and you were so sure—"

"And I was wrong," I said. "I know. I've spent six years knowing. But being wrong once doesn't mean the gift is a lie. It means I misread the pattern. It doesn't mean there are no patterns."

"That's exactly what it means." His voice was low, almost gentle, which made it worse. "For you it does. You can't stop seeing them. And the one time you followed one all the way down, it ruined you."

The dead monitors stared. The stopped clock said 4:47. Somewhere in the building, the storm found a loose seam and made a sound like a held breath.

"Play it again," I said.

"Addie—"

"One more time. And this time, watch the door."

He sat back down, and his hand found the spacebar.

"One more time," he said. "And then I'm walking you to your car, and in the morning the coroner signs the certificate and this is a suicide, because that's what it is."

"Play it."

He played it.

The fifth time, I watched the door. The vault door filled the bottom edge of the frame, gray and massive and shut, its deadbolt thrown. I watched it the way I'd watched the dust, unfocused, letting every frame stack against every other until the differences stood out like pinholes of light.

The door never moved. The bolt never moved. No shadow crossed it, no reflection changed on its painted steel. By every measurable fact, the room was sealed.

But the dust reversed at the seam. The splash arrived nine minutes late. And a man lay dead with a smile on his face and a key that opened nothing I could see.

"Feeding loop," I said.

Frank's hand paused over the keyboard. "What?"

"A feeding loop is how you make a room look occupied when it isn't. You record the room empty, then loop the recording into the live feed. This is the opposite. This is a splice. Someone cut out the part where the man wasn't alone and pasted the edges together so the tape shows solitude from beginning to end. Seventeen minutes of a man alone, assembled out of pieces that were never contiguous."

"The dust—"

"Is the seam. Three frames of wrong air at the cut point. The editor cleaned the footage frame by frame for everything except the dust, because no one watches dust." I looked at him. "And the sea is the clock. Whoever made this film spent hours perfecting the man and forgot to check the water."

Frank stared at the frozen frame. The dead man lay on the floor of the vault, arms out, face tilted to the ceiling, the smile already on him. On the screen it looked like a man who had simply finished.

"Even if you're right," he said at last, his voice quieter, flatter, the voice of a man walking out onto ice and testing it with his weight, "the door was dead-bolted from the inside. The bolt was thrown by hand. No one went in, no one came out. You told me yourself the room is a prison of physical impossibility. So if someone killed him, Addie, how? How does a killer get into a room that can't be entered, kill a man, and get out again, leaving the bolt thrown behind them?"

I didn't have the answer. The shape was in the fog, but the shape didn't have a face yet.

"I don't know," I said. "Not yet. But I know the tape is a lie. And I know the room is the alibi. Which means the answer is in the room, Frank. It has to be. The killer didn't break the room. The killer used it."

He looked at me a long time. The storm worked its way around the building, the glass trembled in its frame, and I could feel the whole weight of the case settling onto the two of us in the dark.

"Okay," he said at last. "Say I believe you. Then the first thing we need is the original. The unedited footage, before someone cut it."

"Where would that live?"

He nodded at the workstation. "Local server. The institute archives every feed to a drive in the basement. If the footage was edited in place, the archive might still hold the source—if the editor didn't scrub it too." He pulled out his phone, already dialing. "I'll get the IT guy down here. If there's a raw file left anywhere in this building, we'll find it tonight."

"And if there isn't?"

"Then we have your dust and your wave," he said, "and a dead man in an impossible room, and a splice with no source. And I'll be right back where I started: vouching for you, with nothing to show for it."

The phone connected. He turned away to talk, voice low and official, and I was left alone in the glass fishbowl with the frozen frame of a dead man and the hum of machinery that had nothing to hide.

I looked at the seam in the wall where the dust had reversed. I looked at the wave that had arrived nine minutes late. And I thought about a room that was a prison of physical impossibility, built to prove exactly one thing.

The room itself was the alibi.

Which meant the answer was in the room.

And I had been in the room, and I had missed it, and I was going to have to go back.
